Amazon SQS Retry with Backoff Strategy using DynamoDB
Before we go into details on retry strategy, let’s first understand two important features Amazon SQS supports and their hard limits.
Visibility Timeout: In simple terms, once the message is consumed for processing by a consumer, it will be visible to other consumers only after the configured visibility timeout (if not deleted). The maximum value for this configuration is 12 hours.
Amazon SQS visibility timeout
Delay Seconds: It is the same as visibility timeout, with the difference that it is applicable only when the message is sent for the first time on the queue for processing. The maximum value for this configuration can be up to 15 minutes.
Amazon SQS delay queues
By default, every time an application fails to process the message, the same message will be visible for processing once the visibility timeout has passed. For example, if the visibility timeout is set to 15 minutes, the application will receive the same message for retrying in the 15th minute, the 30th minute, the 45th minute, and so on.
What we want is that the application should receive the same message for retry on the 15th minute, the 45th minute (15 + 30), the 90th minute (15 + 30 + 45), and so on.
Amazon SQS provides an option to change the visibility timeout of a specific message in a queue to a new value. The new value can be set to 12 hours (the hard limit of visibility timeout).
ChangeMessageVisibility
Here is a sample of code using Change Visibility Timeout to mimic the retry strategy using the Python Boto3 library.
For increasing the retry value based on number of attempts, we are using default message attribute ApproximateReceiveCount provided by SQS (line 20).
ApproximateReceiveCount – Returns the number of times a message has been received across all queues but not deleted.
The above approach assumes that every time a message is ingested by an application, it tries and fails to process it. There may be instances where the application consumed the message but then restarted, erroneously, or otherwise failed to process it. As a result, the value of ApproximateReceiveCount, which counts the number of times a message is ingested (but not really processed), is incorrect, resulting in the incorrect retry time computation.
For the solution to work effectively, instead of using ApproximateReceiveCount, we can use some sort of persistent storage to keep an attempt count for each message. The attempt count could then be used to compute the retry time. In this case, we would be using Amazon DynamoDB to store the message ID and the attempted count.
Screenshot of sample DynamoDB table storing message ID and the attempts value.
